title: A Note on These Essays
paragraphs: I originally wrote these essays for the University of Oxford’s Advanced Philosophy of Physics course, offered by the Department of Philosophy. I took it as a “broadening course” for my DPhil in Mathematics, submitting these two essays as an output in July 2021. I’d like to thank Adam Caulton, who reviewed and gave feedback on drafts of these essays during the course.
To put them into context, I’d like to briefly comment on the inspiration for each one.

The quantum segment of the Advanced Philosophy of Physics course had a number of suggested essay questions, though students could also choose their own. One of these suggested questions was: “Can quantum mechanics under the Everett interpretation be experimentally tested? Can it be confirmed?” Upon reading this, it struck me that it is common to discuss and question the testability of the Everettian (many-worlds) interpretation, but we do not typically subject the same level of scrutiny to the Copenhagen interpretation. So, I thought it would be fun to invert the question, exchanging _Everettian_ for _Copenhagen_ to emphasise the double standards that are typically applied when considering the testability of quantum interpretations.

For the thermodynamics segment, I have long been fascinated by the controversy surrounding whether or not entropy is subjective. The first paper I ever read was “The Gibbs Paradox” by E. T. Jaynes, upon recommendation from my high school physics teacher when he found out I was interested in entropy. I really liked Jaynes’ approach to explaining the anthropomorphic nature of entropy changes using various playful thought experiments, such as inventing fictional gases “whifnium” and “whafnium”.
Then, when reading around the subject during the course, I noticed a pattern: philosophers kept discussing entropy in the context of coffee. To collect a few of these:

“The vast majority of projects in the field in the past century have sought to explain why my coffee (at room temperature) tends to equilibrium by proving that an ensemble has a property evincing monotonic behaviour.”

“Can anybody seriously think that our merely being ignorant of the exact microconditions of thermodynamic systems plays some part in bringing it about, in making it the case, that (say) milk [mixes into] coffee? How could that be? What can all those guys have been up to?”

“(If Albert had asked how our being ignorant of the exact microconditions of the coffee could make it the case that we are unable to un-mix the coffee and the milk, the rhetorical force is at least less clear.) [...] (Even if provided with an exact readout of my coffee’s microstate, I lack the manipulative precision to use that information to unmix it.)”
— Wallace, 2020, “The Necessity of Gibbsian Statistical Mechanics”

Bemused by the frequency of coffee references in such serious academic literature, I upgraded it from an illustrative sidenote in past discourse to the central conceptual tool in my essay, where I give my take on the subjectivity of entropy using a series of (literally) colourful coffee-centred thought experiments.
I am pleased to have these essays now included in this volume of the Bold Conjectures series—best read with a warm cup of coffee!
